module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil
public import FormalConjectures.GreensOpenProblems.«28»

/-!
# Mathoverflow 339137

Why do polynomials with coefficients 0,1
 like to have only factors with 0,1
 coefficients?

*Reference:* [mathoverflow/339137](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/339137)
asked by user [*Sil*](https://mathoverflow.net/users/136794/sil)
-/

@[expose] public section

open scoped Polynomial
namespace Mathoverflow339137

/--
The predicate that all coefficients of a polynomial are either zero or one.
`P.coeffs` is the finite set of all *nonzero* coefficients of the polynomial `P`.
So `IsZeroOne P` means that every nonzero coefficient of `P` is equal to 1.
Note that zero coefficients are not included in `P.coeffs`.
-/
def IsZeroOne (P : ℝ[X]) := P.coeffs ⊆ {1}

-- TODO(lezeau): add statement that coefficients must at least lie in `[0, 1]`

/--
Let $P(x), Q(x) ∈ ℝ[x]$ be two monic polynomials with non-negative coefficients.
If $R(x) = P(x)Q(x)$ is a $0,1$ polynomial (coefficients only from $\{0,1\}$), then $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$
are also $0, 1$ polynomials.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 12]
theorem mathoverflow_339137 (P Q R : ℝ[X]) (hP: P.Monic) (hQ : Q.Monic)
    (hp : ∀ c ∈ P.coeffs, 0 ≤ c) (hq : ∀ c ∈ Q.coeffs, 0 ≤ c)
    (h : R = P * Q) (hR : IsZeroOne R) :
    IsZeroOne P ∧ IsZeroOne Q := by
  sorry

/--
Green's Open Problem 28 is the probabilistic reformulation of Mathoverflow 339137.

Suppose that $X, Y$ are two finitely-supported independent random variables taking integer values,
and such that $X + Y$ is uniformly distributed on its range. Are $X$ and $Y$ themselves uniformly
distributed on their ranges?

Mathematically, this equivalence is established via Probability Generating Functions (PGFs),
shifting the support to $\mathbb{N}$, and appropriately scaling the coefficients.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 60]
theorem mathoverflow_339137_probabilistic :
    type_of% Mathoverflow339137.mathoverflow_339137 ↔ type_of% Green28.green_28 := by
  sorry

end Mathoverflow339137

findings.description:
The right-hand side is `type_of% Green28.green_28`, and `green_28` is `answer(sorry) ↔ G28body`. So what this theorem says depends on how the `answer(sorry)` placeholder is elaborated, not on the mathematics alone.

Under the default `google.answer = always_true`, `answer(sorry)` at `Prop` becomes a bare `True`. The theorem is then `MO ↔ (True ↔ G28body)`, which is the intended and true (textbook, PGF) equivalence `MO ↔ G28body`; I checked this with `#print` and `simp only [true_iff]`.

However:
(i) The repository's own `FormalConjecturesAnswerPostpone` target (lakefile.toml, `weak.google.answer = "postpone"`) compiles the same files. `scripts/extract_names.lean` requires that build to extract answer metadata. Re-elaborating `green_28` under that option in a scratch file shows the theorem becomes `MO ↔ (([mdata answer:true] sorry) ↔ G28body)`. That statement is unprovable, and because the answer annotation is copied in, this `textbook` theorem gets a `Prop` answer slot. Under `with_auxiliary` it is `MO ↔ (green_28._answer ↔ G28body)` with `_answer := sorry`.
(ii) The theorem was added in #2380 on 2026-03-09, before the `always_true` default existed (#3512, 2026-03-14, described as the default "for now"). Before #3512, `answer(sorry)` elaborated to `sorry` (checked in the local git history), so the theorem as added stated `MO ↔ (sorry ↔ G28body)`.
(iii) The theorem is tied to Green 28's answer literal. Suppose `green_28` is filled in with `answer(False)` and this file is not updated at the same time. Then the theorem becomes `MO ↔ (False ↔ G28body)`, i.e. `MO ↔ ¬G28body`, which is false because MO ↔ G28body.

`ErdosProblems/945.lean` documents this limitation: "Because the theorems require `answer(sorry)` we can't handle this with `type_of%`". It factors the body into a `def` instead. The same pattern does appear in `AmicableNumbers.infinitely_many_amicable` and `erdos_287.variants.prime_conjecture_implies`, both added after `always_true`. At this commit, in the default build, the statement is mathematically correct, so this is about robustness, not a misformalization.
findings.source_evidence: MathOverflow 339137 (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/339137), question body: "Probability theory reformulation: An interesting alternative reformulation provided in comments by Gro-Tsen/Rémy Oudompheng: Assume X,Y are independent random variables supported on a finite subset of the integers, and assume Z=X+Y is uniformly distributed on its support: is it necessarily the case that X and Y are themselves uniformly distributed on their support? ... In this form it is also currently stated as Problem 28 in Ben Green's 100 Open Problems." The claim to state is the equivalence of the two formulations, with no answer placeholder in it. Green's Problem 28 (open-problems.pdf) poses the same probabilistic question.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the dependence on the answer slot. For example, in GreensOpenProblems/28.lean add `def Green28.Statement : Prop := ∀ (X Y : PMF ℤ), X.support.Finite ∧ Y.support.Finite ∧ IsUniformOnSupport (indepSum X Y) → IsUniformOnSupport X ∧ IsUniformOnSupport Y` and state `green_28 : answer(sorry) ↔ Green28.Statement`. Then state `theorem mathoverflow_339137_probabilistic : type_of% mathoverflow_339137 ↔ Green28.Statement`. Alternatively, write the `∀ X Y : PMF ℤ, ...` formula out directly on the right-hand side.

reformulations.difference: "0,1 polynomial" is encoded as `IsZeroOne P := P.coeffs ⊆ {1}`, and "non-negative coefficients" as `∀ c ∈ P.coeffs, 0 ≤ c`. Mathlib's `Polynomial.coeffs` is the finset of *nonzero* coefficients (`p.support.image p.coeff`), so a reader may think `⊆ {1}` wrongly leaves out 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A coefficient not in `P.coeffs` is 0. So `P.coeffs ⊆ {1}` says every coefficient is 0 or 1, and `∀ c ∈ P.coeffs, 0 ≤ c` says every coefficient is ≥ 0. I proved both in Lean: `IsZeroOne P ↔ ∀ n, P.coeff n = 0 ∨ P.coeff n = 1` and `(∀ c ∈ P.coeffs, 0 ≤ c) ↔ ∀ n, 0 ≤ P.coeff n`, using `coeff_mem_coeffs` and `mem_coeffs_iff`. The rest (ℝ[X], `Monic`, `R = P * Q`, both conclusions) matches the MO conjecture word for word.

reformulations.difference: In the default build the elaborated statement is `MO ↔ (True ↔ G28body)`, not `MO ↔ G28body`. The `True` is what `answer(sorry)` in `green_28` becomes under `always_true`. The build-dependence is covered by the questionable finding.
reformulations.equivalence_argument:
`(True ↔ B) ↔ B`. In Lean, `simp only [true_iff]` proves `type_of% mathoverflow_339137_probabilistic ↔ (MO ↔ G28body)`, with both sides written out. `MO ↔ G28body` is the equivalence the source asserts, and it is true.
(⇒) Let X, Y have finite supports and X+Y be uniform on s. Let a, A be the min and max of supp X, and b, B those of supp Y. Put P(t) = Σ_i X(a+i)/X(A) tⁱ, and Q likewise. Both are monic with non-negative coefficients, and the coefficient of t^m in PQ is (X+Y)(a+b+m)/(X(A)Y(B)). Since (X+Y)(A+B) = X(A)Y(B) > 0 must equal 1/|s|, PQ is a 0-1 polynomial. MO then makes P and Q 0-1, so X and Y are uniform on their supports.
(⇐) Put X(k) = p_k/P(1) and Y(k) = q_k/Q(1); P(1), Q(1) ≥ 1. Then X+Y has mass r_n/R(1), which is uniform on supp R. Green 28 makes X uniform, so p_k ∈ {0, P(1)/|supp X|}, and the leading coefficient 1 forces this value to be 1.
I checked in Lean that `Green28.indepSum X Y n = ∑' x, X x * Y (n - x)` and that `uniformOfFinset` has the expected values.
